Mufflers
MUF-lerz
noun
From Old French moufle, a covering; rendering Hebrew re‘ālōth, the fluttering, spangled half-veils of the daughters of Zion (Isa 3:19).

Biblical Definition

Mufflers are the light, trembling veils — spangled half-coverings that fluttered before the face — named in the second line of the inventory: “The chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers” (Isa 3:19). The Hebrew suggests a shimmering, quivering thing, a veil worn not to hide the face but to advertise it — concealment turned coquetry. Here the inventory touches something subtler than gold: the fashion that plays at modesty. A true covering says, this beauty is kept for its covenant place; the muffler of Zion’s daughters said, guess. It belonged to the same walk as the “wanton eyes” and the mincing steps (Isa 3:16) — a wardrobe of suggestion, veiling as performance. The LORD is not mocked by fabric: He reads the message of a garment as surely as the message of a tongue, and He listed the mufflers with the rest of the bravery to be taken away in a day. Let the believer learn that modesty is a matter of intent before it is a matter of inches. Rebekah took a vail to meet her bridegroom in honest reverence (Gen 24:65); Zion’s daughters took a shimmer to the street. The garment may be cousin; the hearts are strangers. God weighs what the clothing is saying, and to whom.

Webster 1828 Definition

The spangled, fluttering half-veils of Zion’s daughters — concealment turned coquetry; God reads the message of a garment.

MUFFLERS, light trembling veils; spangled half-coverings fluttering before the face.

Named in the inventory of Zion’s finery: chains, bracelets, and mufflers (Isa 3:19).

A veil worn not to hide the face but to advertise it — veiling as performance.

They belong to the same walk as the wanton eyes and mincing steps of Isaiah 3:16.

Rebekah’s vail meant reverence; the muffler meant “guess.”

Key Scripture

Isa 3:19 — "The chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers,"

Isa 3:16 — "Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:"

Gen 24:65 — "For she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself."

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

Modern Corruption

The muffler names the oldest fashion trick — modesty worn as suggestion; the age has made veiling-as-performance an entire industry.

expand to see more

The corruption is performance dressed as propriety. The muffler kept the letter of the veil and inverted its spirit — covering as a lure — and the present age has built industries on the same inversion: the calculated tease marketed as empowerment, garments engineered to say guess while claiming to say no.

The recovered principle is intent before inches. Modesty is not a hemline arithmetic but a heart’s message: Rebekah’s vail honored a bridegroom; the muffler advertised a wearer. Women professing godliness adorn themselves with shamefacedness and sobriety (1Ti 2:9) — and men of God keep their own wardrobe of suggestion under the same law, for the LORD reads what clothing says, and to whom.

Hebrew Roots

From the Old French for a covering, mufflers render the spangled quivering veils of Isaiah 3 — concealment inverted into coquetry.

expand to see more

Mufflers — Old French moufle; Hebrew re‘ālōth, tremblers.

Spangled half-veils fluttering before the face (Isa 3:19).

Veiling worn to advertise, not to honor.

Cousin in fabric to Rebekah’s vail; stranger in heart (Gen 24:65).

Modesty is intent before it is inches (1Ti 2:9).

Usage
